Dynamic programming approach is often employed specifically when solving a category of problems with **Overlapping Subproblems.**This implies that the problem can be split in into subproblems and the subproblems can be repetitive i.e the same sub problem can show up seveal times within the context of the same problem solution.

Additionally this family of problem also has the O**ptimal Substructure** property i.e an optimal solution for the problem can be constructed from optimal solutions of its subproblems.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Problem is continualy split into sub problems until a base case is reached

There are two approaches to solving this class of problems.

**Top-Down — Memoization :**

This approach employs a recursive strategy to split the problem into subproblems until it reaches a base case i.e no further partioning is feasible. It then optimises the computation by storing results of each subproblem in a table thus preventing any redundant computations to repetitive subproblems encountered later. In other words before solving a sub problem , we check the results computed so far to determine if this sub problem was already solved and if so we just use the previously computed result and move on instead of recomputing.

13.1 Introduction

Today we’re going to do a couple more examples of dynamic programming. While the particular problems that we’re going to talk about are important and very nice, we’re spending a class on them not so much because of their inherent interest, but to see some more examples of dynamic programming. Since last class I mentioned the usefulness of dynamic programming in string algo- rithms, we’re first going to talk about the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem. Then, since we’ve spent some time recently on binary search trees, we’re going to talk about the Optimal Binary Search Tree problem.

13.2 Longest Common Subsequence

13.2.1 Definitions
While there are many notions of similarity between strings, and many problems that we would like to optimize over strings, a natural problem (and notion of similarity) is the Longest Common Subsequence.
